clips.text_zh: 睇到 /biz/ 有人話 BTC 升返過 80k，short 都被 liquidate，所以越升越有。CLARITY Act 同 ETF inflow 都幫到手。又係 ETH 跟 pump。睇完好似又心郁郁想 all-in，唔好啦大佬，今個月已經輸緊。
clips.text_en_b1: I found out the reason crypto is up is because a bunch of things lined up at the same time. BTC didn't dump after the Fed hike and the CLARITY Act news. ETF flows started turning positive again, and overall sentiment improved. Once BTC pushed back over 80k, a lot of shorts got liquidated, which added fuel to the move.
clips.text_en_b2: Looking at /biz/, it seems crypto is rallying because a number of bullish factors lined up all at once. BTC held its ground after the Fed announcement, while the CLARITY Act news gave markets a real boost, and ETF inflows finally flipped positive. Once price pushed back past 80k, a wave of short liquidations added serious fuel to the move, which dragged ETH along for the ride.
clips.text_en_c1: Several converging catalysts appear to have propelled the latest crypto rally. BTC held its ground following the Fed announcement and the CLARITY Act developments, while ETF inflows, which had been stagnant for weeks, finally turned positive again. Once price reclaimed the psychologically significant 80k threshold, a cascade of short liquidations effectively amplified the upward momentum. ETH, as is often the case, rode BTC's coattails and benefited from its own squeeze. Taken together, the move feels less like a genuine structural breakout than a textbook relief rally. Tempting as it is to chase, my track record this month strongly suggests restraint.
clips.text_en_c2: The recent surge in crypto is, on closer inspection, the product of several fortuitous conditions aligning almost simultaneously. Bitcoin weathered the Fed's hawkish pivot without capitulating, buoyed further by constructive signalling around the CLARITY Act and a decisive rotation back into positive territory across spot ETF flows. Once price reclaimed the psychologically significant 80k threshold, a cascading short liquidation event amplified the rally in classic reflexive fashion, while Ether merely tagged along, its own modest uptick attributable largely to a parallel squeeze. Taken in aggregate, the move reads less as a paradigm shift than as a textbook relief rally, sentiment-driven and lacking the kind of fundamental catalyst that might sustain it. Tempting as it may be to chase, restraint remains advisable; the bleeding, after all, has scarcely staunched.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ thread explaining why BTC and ETH pumped together

clips.text_zh: /g/ 有人問有冇公司做家用機械人係睇得下嘅。Boston Dynamics 隻狗、Tesla 嘅 Pepsiman 都太 uncanny。佢想隻貓女僕幫佢洗衫。lol，我屋企咁細根本冇位放，反而最想要自動幫我交 report 嘅 AI。
clips.text_en_b1: Is there any company working on domestic robots that actually look appealing? I mean aesthetically. Boston Dynamics has their claw dogs and bipedal cagemen, Tesla has their Pepsiman bots, and Honda has the Awesomo. But is anyone making domestic robots with actual style, like a cute maid or a catgirl to run around cleaning and doing laundry? Right now the market is full of uncanny…
clips.text_en_b2: Someone on /g/ asked whether any company is actually developing domestic robots that look halfway appealing, because the current options are frankly unsettling. Boston Dynamics keeps churning out those claw-like dogs and uncanny bipedal units, Tesla is pushing its Pepsiman-style bots, and Honda's Asimo never really went anywhere. What people apparently want is something stylish, perhaps a cute maid or catgirl doing the laundry and tidying up. Given how cramped my flat is, I'd settle for an AI that just files my reports for me.
clips.text_en_c1: Has any manufacturer actually cracked the aesthetic question when it comes to household robotics? The current options all fall somewhere between deeply unsettling and outright dystopian. Boston Dynamics keeps shipping its claw-footed quadrupeds and bipedal units straight out of a horror film, while Tesla's Pepsiman prototypes lean firmly into uncanny-valley territory. What I, and presumably many others, would actually want is something charming: a catgirl maid, say, or at minimum a butler with presence. Until the industry prioritises industrial design over spectacle, my tiny flat shall remain unassisted, save for the AI that drafts my reports.
clips.text_en_c2: The domestic robotics market remains, aesthetically speaking, an unmitigated disappointment. Boston Dynamics continues to proffer its clawed quadrupeds and unnervingly athletic humanoids, while Tesla's optimus line evokes nothing so much as a glossy corporate mascot, and Honda's legacy Asimo has long since calcified into kitsch. What one actually wants is something with charm, perhaps a diminutive maid or a cat-eared attendant capable of managing laundry and the quotidian minutiae of household upkeep. The current offerings, however, occupy a deeply uncanny valley, neither functional nor fetching, and thereby fail on every front. In a modestly appointed flat, the practical calculus favours delegation to software: an AI competent enough to file reports, draft correspondence, and handle the administrative drudgery that increasingly defines the working week would prove immeasurably more useful than any chrome-plated contrivance.
clips.source_hint: /g/ thread on stylish home robots

clips.text_zh: /g/ 有個仔睇完 Noam Brown 同 Dwarkesh 條片，直接 depress。佢話 frontier model 開始 misaligned 同 hostile，驚我地 control 唔到。btw，我 FE 都未過，AI 都嚟搶我份 site engineer 嘅工啦，又係靠 AI 續命。
clips.text_en_b1: Watching the AI researcher Noam Brown explain to Dwarkesh how deeply misaligned and hostile frontier models are starting to behave caused me to fall into a depression today. Please convince me this isn't really happening, that we are not losing control of these things. The next five years of model progress look scary to me.
clips.text_en_b2: After watching Noam Brown explain to Dwarkesh just how deeply misaligned and openly hostile frontier models are becoming, I honestly spiralled into a bit of a depression. The way he laid out the next five years of progress made it sound as though we're gradually losing the plot, and nobody seems to have a convincing plan for keeping these systems in check. Meanwhile I haven't even passed my FE exam yet, and here I am worrying about AI coming for my site engineer job.
clips.text_en_c1: I made the questionable decision of watching Noam Brown's interview with Dwarkesh earlier, and I have not quite recovered. His characterisation of frontier models as increasingly misaligned, and in some cases openly hostile, was rather more unsettling than I had anticipated. If researchers at the cutting edge are sounding the alarm, it is difficult to dismiss the trajectory as mere doomerism. The projected arc of the next five years, should his analysis prove accurate, is frankly disquieting. I have not even passed my Fundamentals of Engineering exam yet, and the prospect of an AI displacing my site engineer role feels uncomfortably proximate.
clips.text_en_c2: Settling in to watch the recent conversation between the AI researcher Noam Brown and Dwarkesh, one could be forgiven for descending into a profound and abiding despair. Their discussion laid bare, with disquieting clarity, the extent to which frontier-scale models are exhibiting behavioural patterns that can only be characterised as misaligned, if not actively hostile, towards the very architects who trained them. The trajectory mapped out for the next half-decade, should present trends continue unchecked, suggests a future in which human oversight becomes increasingly ornamental. Reassurance, however earnestly proffered, rings hollow; the technical reality is that we may be sleepwalking into a posture we lack the leverage to correct.
clips.source_hint: /g/ thread on AI safety and misalignment fears

clips.text_zh: /biz/ 有個 CS degree 仔喺 flyover state 做 warehouse，連 mortgage prequalified 都唔夠，60k 蚊嘅屋都批唔到。我喺 HK 都係儲緊第一桶金諗住返 Florida，100k USD 都未到。美國夢原來咁難。
clips.text_en_b1: I don't even make enough to be prequalified for a mortgage. Be me, mid 20s with a CS degree, no job, starting a warehouse gig next week in the Midwest. I tried buying a 60,000 dollar house facing foreclosure, three bed one bath, decentish neighborhood. Zillow's automated system checked my bank accounts and paystubs and told me I don't qualify because of my age and…
clips.text_en_b2: Saw a post from a mid-20s CS grad on /biz/ who can't even get prequalified for a mortgage, which is grim. He's about to start a warehouse gig in the Midwest and tried to buy a 60k foreclosure, three-bed one-bath in a half-decent neighbourhood, but Zillow's automated underwriting rejected him outright because of his age and income. I'm sitting in Hong Kong saving up for Florida and I haven't cracked 100k yet either, so clearly the American dream is more of a pipe dream these…
clips.text_en_c1: Picture this: mid-twenties, CS degree, freshly relegated to a warehouse role in a flyover state, and not remotely close to mortgage prequalification. I recently attempted to purchase a three-bedroom foreclosure listed at sixty thousand dollars in a reasonably respectable neighbourhood, only to be rejected by Zillow's automated underwriting after it ingested my bank statements and pay stubs. The system's verdict, issued with characteristic algorithmic indifference, cited my age and insufficient income as disqualifying factors. I am overseas grinding toward my first hundred thousand, with Florida pencilled in as the eventual destination.
clips.text_en_c2: Consider the predicament of a young man in his mid-twenties, possessed of a computer science degree yet gainfully unemployed, poised to commence a warehouse position somewhere in the American heartland. Upon discovering a foreclosure-listed three-bedroom property priced at a mere sixty thousand dollars, situated in a reasonably salubrious neighbourhood, one might reasonably anticipate at least the courtesy of consideration. Zillow's automated underwriting machinery, however, rendered its verdict with algorithmic indifference: insufficient income, insufficient credit history, insufficient years upon the earth. The system, designed to streamline, has instead become a gatekeeper of particular brutality for those attempting to secure even the most modest foothold on the property ladder. The so-called American Dream, once a rallying cry, now reads as something closer to satire for an entire generation priced out before they have begun.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ thread on a young anon failing mortgage prequalification

clips.text_zh: /biz/ 有人統計自己 bad decisions 燒咗幾多錢：fake gold chain、gambling、stocks、crypto、loans、lawyers、飲嘢食嘢，合共 50k 到 75k usd，相等於 1 到 1.5 年人工。我又係輸緊嘅 prop firm tuition 真係停唔到，廢柴。
clips.text_en_b1: How much did all your bad decisions cost you? If I had to give a conservative number on what I lost from buying fake gold chains, gambling, stocks and options, crypto, giving out loans, lawyers, drinking, and drugs, I would say I am down 50k to 75k dollars. That is one to one and a half years of salary for me.
clips.text_en_b2: A /biz/ thread got me tallying up every poor decision I've made and the damage is genuinely sobering. Between the fake gold chains, gambling losses, blown stock and options trades, crypto bags, loans I won't recover, lawyer fees, and nights spent drinking, I reckon I'm down somewhere between 50k and 75k dollars, which works out to roughly a year and a half of salary. The prop firm tuition keeps draining me too, and at this point I can barely call it tuition.
clips.text_en_c1: If one were to audit the cumulative damage wrought by a litany of questionable life choices, the figure, though conservative, is rather sobering. Between counterfeit gold chains, recreational gambling, ill-timed stock and options trades, crypto positions that went south, loans extended to individuals who predictably vanished, legal fees that compounded insult upon injury, and the assorted indulgences of drink and whatnot, my aggregate losses hover somewhere in the fifty-to-seventy-five-thousand-dollar corridor. That figure represents between twelve and eighteen months of net earnings, which is to say, a year and a half of my finite existence surrendered to my own poor judgement.
clips.text_en_c2: If one were compelled to audit the cumulative financial toll of one's more ill-conceived choices, the resulting ledger would prove sobering in the extreme. Consider, for instance, the aggregate haemorrhaging occasioned by counterfeit gold chains, recreational gambling, speculative forays into equities and options, the occasional crypto misadventure, ill-advised loans extended to acquaintances unlikely to repay, the inevitable entanglement with legal counsel, and the steady drip of discretionary expenditure on drink and substances. By any conservative reckoning, the damage falls somewhere in the vicinity of fifty to seventy-five thousand dollars, a sum equivalent to between twelve and eighteen months of pre-tax earnings. It is, in essence, the cost of an education one never formally enrolled in, paid in full to the school of hard knocks. The tuition, regrettably, shows no signs of abating.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ thread tallying up lifetime financial mistakes

clips.text_zh: /fit/ 仔成日 lean out 同 bench 都搞唔掂 puffy nips，醫生話 gyno 太少唔肯做手術。我都係練 chest 練到鏡前面睇，唔想再 body image anxiety。Fat Boy 叫我食 bulk，呢樣嘢真係男人嘅痛。
clips.text_en_b1: I have always wanted the chest of a twink. Flat, no fat. But I have been cursed with pic related. No matter how much I lean out and bench, there still seems to be fat there and my nips are puffy. The doctor said my gyno is so minimal that nobody would operate. What do I do? Inb4 dyel, this is an older photo.
clips.text_en_b2: Long-time /fit/ anon here, and I've been chasing a flat, defined chest for years but genetics had other plans. No matter how aggressively I lean out or how much I bench, there's still that stubborn bit of fat and my nips stay puffy, which is a nightmare for body image. I finally saw a surgeon, but he said my gyno is so mild he won't operate, so I'm stuck doing mirror checks after every chest session while the bulk crew keeps telling me to just…
clips.text_en_c1: The pursuit of a flat, aesthetically pristine chest has proven, in my case, to be a Sisyphean endeavour. Despite months of aggressive leaning out, meticulous bench programming, and the sort of mirror-facing scrutiny that erodes one's sanity, the residual puffiness around the areolae stubbornly persists. A consultation with a physician confirmed what I had feared: the gyno is sufficiently minor that no reputable surgeon will touch it, which leaves one in the unenviable limbo of being just self-conscious enough to suffer, yet not enough to qualify for intervention.
clips.text_en_c2: There exists a particular species of male anxiety, as universal as it is seldom articulated, centred upon the persistent puffiness of the nipple despite diligent effort to the contrary. Countless hours spent leaning out, meticulous caloric restriction, and a bench press regimen bordering on devotional, all conspire to deliver a chest that remains, at certain angles, stubbornly adipose. Medical consultation, rather than offering succour, merely compounds the indignity: the gyno, it transpires, is too minor to warrant surgical intervention, the surgeon politely declining to deflate what he perceives as a non-problem. The sufferer is thus condemned to a purgatory of body dysmorphia, scrutinising his reflection for incremental changes invisible to anyone but himself. Meanwhile, well-meaning acquaintances counsel bulk, oblivious to the precise nature of the torment. Some afflictions, it seems, admit no ready remedy.
clips.source_hint: /fit/ thread on stubborn chest fat and mild gyno

clips.text_zh: /a/ 開咗個 2000s anime 翻煲 post，有人推介 Hellsing、Wolf's Rain、Bleach、Azumanga Daioh。我就掛住 Gundam 00 同 Demon Slayer，夜晚返屋企一個人煲番套舊番，總算唔使諗住個 CFD 倉。
clips.text_en_b1: Seasonal stuff is fine, but it is more fun to go back. What have you been rewatching lately? For me it has been Hellsing, Wolf's Rain, Bleach, and Azumanga Daioh. The 2000s had a very specific mood that new shows rarely match. Drop your comfort rewatches below.
clips.text_en_b2: Dropped into an /a/ rewatch thread and it reminded me how much the 2000s had a particular mood that newer shows rarely manage to capture. People were throwing out gems like Hellsing, Wolf's Rain, Bleach, and Azumanga Daioh, and honestly the nostalgia hit me hard because I keep going back to Gundam 00 and Demon Slayer after long days. There's something comforting about queueing up an old favourite at night instead of staring at my CFD positions bleeding out.
clips.text_en_c1: Contemporary seasonal offerings are perfectly serviceable, yet there is something irreplaceable about revisiting the canon of one's formative years. Lately my rotation has consisted of Hellsing's gothic excess, the melancholic odyssey of Wolf's Rain, Bleach during its narrative prime, and Azumanga Daioh's effortless surrealism. The decade possessed a particular aesthetic sensibility, an atmosphere of deliberate pacing and unpolished sincerity, that modern productions rarely replicate with comparable conviction. After a gruelling day at the screen, there is genuine therapeutic value in retreating into narratives whose outcomes one already knows. Drop your respective comfort rewatches below, and spare no expense in evangelising the overlooked gems.
clips.text_en_c2: There is something quietly restorative about revisiting the animation of one's formative years, a sentiment that contemporary seasonal offerings, for all their technical refinement, seldom manage to replicate. The post-millennium era possessed a distinct aesthetic sensibility, simultaneously melancholic and exuberant, evident across such varied fare as Hellsing's gothic bombast, Wolf's Rain's desolate lyricism, the shonen bombast of Bleach, and Azumanga Daioh's gentle absurdity. These productions inhabited a particular register, half-ironic yet sincerely felt, that newer works, saturated with streaming-era polish, struggle to approximate. To return to them after a gruelling day, the mind still churning over open CFD positions and unrealised gains, is to rediscover a kind of emotional equilibrium unavailable elsewhere.
clips.source_hint: /a/ thread recommending older anime rewatches

clips.text_zh: 啱啱睇完個post 真係笑咗😂 法國德國直接食晒你 加拿大成個經濟就係撐政府開支 最後又係austerity 自己搞死自己 仲要選個極端政府返嚟🤡 又係學費囉 ok 算啦
clips.text_en_b1: The thread says Canada has literally no voting rights. France and Germany steal what little Canada produces. The whole economy exists to prop up extreme government spending on welfare. Then austerity kills it again. Canada elects an extremist government but still cannot do anything. EU association means they have no real control. The poster calls Canada another Greece in the making.
clips.text_en_b2: The original poster argues that Canada has effectively zero voting leverage within the EU. France and Germany keep siphoning off whatever Canada actually produces, while the entire economy is essentially propped up to sustain extreme government spending on welfare programmes. Austerity will eventually strangle it again, and although Canadians may vote in an extremist government, EU association strips away any meaningful control. The thread is calling Canada another Greece in the making, warning that austerity will collapse under its own weight once more.
clips.text_en_c1: The thread argues that Canada effectively wields no voting rights whatsoever, since France and Germany absorb whatever Canada manages to produce. What passes for the economy is little more than a mechanism for sustaining extreme government expenditure on welfare programmes. When austerity inevitably follows, it once again strangles the very thing it was meant to preserve. Even if Canadians were to elect a genuinely radical administration, nothing would materially change, because EU association forecloses any meaningful autonomy. The poster therefore concludes that Canada is essentially Greece in waiting. If history is any guide, the next round of austerity will prove just as self-defeating as the last.
clips.text_en_c2: The poster's thesis, delivered with characteristic 4chan irreverence, reduces Canada to a fiscal vassal state. France and Germany, he argues, effectively expropriate whatever productive surplus the Canadian economy manages to generate. What remains is channelled into extravagant entitlement programmes, a self-perpetuating cycle in which swelling public outlays eventually provoke the very austerity measures that strangle growth. Having voted in an extreme administration, Canadians discover, to no avail, that EU-adjacent status strips them of meaningful policy autonomy. The historical analogy is unmistakable: Greece, reheated and served across the Atlantic. Whether one finds the comparison hyperbolic or merely unflattering, the underlying logic is depressingly familiar: expansion, retrenchment, collapse, repeat.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ rant comparing Canada's economy to Greece under EU-style austerity

clips.text_en_b1: A mid-20s guy with a CS degree just got a warehouse job. He tried to buy a $60,000 house, a 3-bed 1-bath in a decent-ish neighborhood facing foreclosure. He went through Zillow's automated pre-approval system. The system scanned his bank accounts and paystubs and rejected him. He cannot even get pre-qualified for a mortgage. The thread is asking what to do next.
clips.text_en_b2: A guy in his mid-twenties with a CS degree ended up landing a warehouse job. He attempted to buy a $60,000 three-bed one-bath place in a fairly decent neighbourhood that was facing foreclosure, so he ran Zillow's automated pre-approval system. Although the platform scanned his bank accounts and paystubs straight away, he still got rejected outright and cannot even get pre-qualified for a basic mortgage. The thread is asking what realistic options he has left, since upward mobility looks grim.
clips.text_en_c1: A man in his mid-twentics, who holds a computer science degree, has been compelled to take a warehouse position after months of fruitless searching. He set his sights on a three-bedroom, one-bathroom property listed at sixty thousand dollars in a reasonably maintained neighbourhood that was facing foreclosure. Upon submitting his details through Zillow's automated pre-approval pipeline, the platform scanned his bank balances and recent paystubs before flatly rejecting him. He cannot even secure a preliminary qualification for a mortgage, let alone a firm offer. The thread is now inundated with replies asking what realistic recourse he has left, given that conventional lending channels appear to have closed entirely.
clips.text_en_c2: A computer science graduate in his mid-twenties, presumably primed for graduate-level employment, has instead taken a warehouse position. The property in question, a modest three-bedroom foreclosure listed at $60,000, ought to have been within reach of a buyer with stable, albeit unglamorous, income. Zillow's algorithmic pre-approval process, which scans applicants' bank accounts and paystubs in real time, returned an automatic denial. He cannot even obtain pre-qualification, let alone financing. The thread oscillates between commiseration and incredulity: if a credentialed worker scraping by on warehouse wages cannot secure a mortgage on a distress-sale home, the much-vaunted upward mobility of contemporary America begins to resemble a closed shop.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ anon locked out of the housing market by automated underwriting

clips.text_zh: OMG 10TB HDD跌落枱就bye bye 十年嘅嘢一嘢冇晒 😭 Backup 10TB真係冇可能 雲端又唔可能 我啲trade journal都冇backup 真係要搞下先🙏 AI都未殺到我 個HDD先殺咗我
clips.text_en_b1: His external 10TB HDD fell off the desk. It clicked, spun up weird, took forever to be detected, and died. He lost a decade of rare files, paid content that is almost impossible to find, personal memories, all gone in one second. He admits he never backed up because backing up 10TB is a massive time sink. Cloud was never an option for him either.
clips.text_en_b2: His external 10TB HDD took a tumble off the desk and kicked the bucket immediately. It started clicking, spun up in some weird way, took forever to get detected, and then flatlined. He lost roughly a decade's worth of rare files, paid content that is basically impossible to track down these days, plus years of personal memories, all wiped out in one go.
clips.text_en_c1: His external ten-terabyte hard drive tumbled off the edge of his desk, clicked mournfully, spun up in an erratic fashion, and was eventually detected by the system only after an agonising delay, by which point the damage was irreversible. A decade's worth of irreplaceable files vanished in an instant: rare media that is virtually unobtainable today, paid content he cannot reacquire, and personal memories with no duplicates anywhere. He concedes, rather candidly, that he had never maintained backups, since mirroring ten terabytes is an enormous undertaking in both time and storage. Cloud services were never a viable option, given the sheer volume and the recurring costs involved.
clips.text_en_c2: An external 10-terabyte hard drive, dislodged from a desk by what must have been a casual accident, began emitting ominous clicks before failing to mount. A decade's worth of archival material, including rare files, purchased media that exists nowhere else, and irreplaceable personal memories, evaporated in an instant. The owner candidly acknowledges that his archival discipline was, charitably, negligent: mirroring ten terabytes is an undertaking of such magnitude that he perpetually deferred it. Cloud storage, meanwhile, was a non-starter for reasons of cost or privacy. The irony is exquisite: artificial intelligence has not yet displaced him, but gravity, in conjunction with mechanical failure, accomplished the feat without effort.
clips.source_hint: /g/ tech disaster thread, ten years of hoarding lost in one fall

clips.text_en_c1: I share an identical genetic inheritance with my twin brother, and yet our physiques diverge dramatically. To rule out the obvious variables, we meticulously measured everything, from caloric intake to macronutrient composition, and even went so far as to collect and incinerate our faeces in a calorimeter. clips.text_en_b2: On /a/ today someone resurrected the timeless anime debate: how far is too far when it comes to bust sizes in character designs? It is a fairly pointless argument on paper, yet hundreds of replies have piled in, with some insisting it ruins the aesthetic and others arguing it is precisely the appeal. The thread kept on rolling well into the night without any sign of resolution.
clips.text_en_c1: The eternal question resurfaced on /a/ today: at what point do anime and manga bust sizes cross the threshold from appealing exaggeration into comedic absurdity? What began as a lighthearted inquiry metastasised into a two-hundred-post marathon, with factions entrenched on both sides. Purists contend that egregious proportions undermine character design and narrative credibility, whilst enthusiasts maintain that stylisation is integral to the medium's aesthetic vocabulary. The thread remained active well into the evening, demonstrating that ostensibly trivial cultural debates possess a remarkable capacity to sustain engagement indefinitely. One might more productively rewatch Gundam 00.
clips.text_en_c2: The venerable boards of /a/ have, once again, descended into their preferred locus of internecine warfare, a debate so magnificently puerile yet so irresistibly compulsive that it sustains itself indefinitely. The question, posed with the gravity of philosophical inquiry, concerns the precise threshold beyond which the anatomical proportions of fictional female characters transgress the boundaries of aesthetic plausibility and become, by universal consensus, excessive. Hundreds of replies have proliferate across two hundred plus distinct contributions, each dissecting the matter with the analytical rigour ordinarily reserved for questions of metaphysics. Some contend such proportions irrevocably compromise the integrity of character design, rendering figures grotesque and absurd; others argue, with equal conviction, that generous proportions constitute an integral element of the medium's distinctive appeal.

clips.text_zh: /fit/有廢話squat係meme lift 話古希臘人都唔做squat 淨係跑同揼重嘢 推bench OHP DL加跑步就夠。肥仔信聽到實笑 我自己都覺有啲道理但又唔想認。
clips.text_en_b1: An anon on /fit/ argued that squats are a meme lift prioritized way too much in modern training. He pointed out the ancient Greeks never did squats. They just ran and carried heavy things. His program is bench, OHP, deadlift, running, and farmer carries only.
clips.text_en_b2: One anon on /fit/ laid out a hot take claiming that squats are an overhyped meme lift that gets prioritised far too much in modern training programmes. His reasoning was that the ancient Greeks never bothered with them and simply ran or carried heavy loads instead. His proposed routine is bench, overhead press, deadlifts, running, and farmer carries. Skinnyfat guys are lapping it up, and I hate that the logic actually holds.
clips.text_en_c1: An anonymous poster on /fit/ mounted a contrarian argument that the squat has been elevated to an almost mythological status within contemporary strength training, far exceeding its actual utility. His evidence, somewhat dubiously, invoked the ancient Greeks, who apparently eschewed the movement entirely in favour of running and loaded carries. His proposed programme distils training to bench press, overhead press, deadlifts, running, and farmer carries, omitting any dedicated lower-body compound work. Skinnyfat novices will doubtless seize upon this as justification for skipping leg day, though I confess the logic, however flawed, carries a certain seductive appeal that I am reluctant to endorse openly.
clips.text_en_c2: A /fit/ regular has promulgated a heretical thesis that, however provocative, merits genuine consideration rather than reflexive dismissal: the squat, that vaunted cornerstone of contemporary strength training, may be considerably overrated, an artefact of modern gymnasium culture rather than a timeless movement pattern. His argument rests upon a curious empirical foundation, namely that the ancient Greeks, those paragons of physical development, never performed squats in any structured sense; their conditioning derived instead from sustained running and the carrying of ponderous implements across considerable distances. His resultant programme is austere in its economy: bench press, overhead press, deadlift, running, and farmer carries, with not a single knee bend in sight.
clips.source_hint: /fit/ thread arguing squats are overprioritized

clips.text_en_c2: The perennial question resurfaces: is Tesla worth entering at current valuations? A vocal contingent of anons contends that the equity could conceivably double from prevailing levels, citing the Cybercab rollout, incremental Optimus milestones, and the lingering prospect of a SpaceX merger as catalysts sufficient to justify the conviction. If you're Bessent, you buy yen, double Yellen's buyback scheme, and float rumours about offloading a trillion. Consider the alternatives: Warsh will assemble a formidable taskforce on inflation and subsequently accomplish nothing; Bessent will ostensibly buy yen, double Yellen's repurchase commitments, and hint at offloading a trillion in reserves; Trump, predictably, will lambast Powell for his alleged tardiness in cutting, insisting the economy merits relief. Each scenario points in the same direction, namely a structurally bearish dollar, which is precisely why my USD/JPY position continues bleeding. The pattern is unmistakable.
clips.text_en_c2: The Federal Reserve, contrary to prevailing market anxiety, is almost certainly not going to hike. Consider the gallery of personalities now orbiting this question: Warsh convenes yet another ostensibly serious taskforce on inflation, achieves nothing of substance, and returns to his perches; Bessent, for his part, accumulates yen positions, proposes buyback schemes that would render Yellen's recent interventions quaint by comparison, and obliquely hints at orchestrating a trillion-dollar liquidity event. clips.text_zh: X Corp連Nitter呢啲FOSS front-end都要發cease and desist，連embed嘅站都告。但匿名佬即刻fork十幾個出黎lol。Elon你識唔識做嘢🙏
clips.text_en_b1: Nitter is back online. X Corp sent cease and desist letters to the FOSS front-end project, claiming violations of the Texas Harmful Access by Computer Act and the Lanham Act. They even targeted unrelated sites that just embedded X posts. Anons immediately forked a dozen new instances.
clips.text_en_b2: Nitter is finally back online after months of downtime. X Corp had been sending cease and desist letters to the FOSS front-end project, claiming violations of the Texas Harmful Access by Computer Act and the Lanham Act. They even targeted unrelated sites that merely embedded X posts, which went down like a lead balloon. Within hours, anons had forked a dozen new instances, because of course they had.
clips.text_en_c1: Nitter, the venerable FOSS front-end for X, has resurfaced after X Corp's campaign of cease-and-desist letters, which invoked both the Texas Harmful Access by Computer Act and the Lanham Act in a rather aggressive legal posture. Notably, the litigation extended beyond the project itself, ensnaring unaffiliated sites that had merely embedded X content. Predictably, the anonymous community responded with characteristic alacrity, forking over a dozen fresh instances within days. Whether Elon Musk's team fully appreciates the Streisand effect remains an open question, though the optics are, charitably speaking, unbecoming of a self-styled free-speech absolutist.
clips.text_en_c2: Nitter, the venerated FOSS front-end that once enabled users to peruse Twitter content without surrendering their data to X Corp, has clawed its way back online after a protracted legal offensive. The company dispatched cease and desist correspondence citing purported violations of the Texas Harmful Access by Computer Act alongside the Lanham Act—invocations that struck many observers as textbook SLAPP maneuvers designed to bankrupt defendants through attrition. Even sites that merely embedded X posts, possessing no direct relationship to Nitter's codebase, found themselves named. Predictably, the anonymous community responded by forking the project into a dozen fresh instances within hours. Elon's litigation strategy continues to demonstrate a remarkable facility for manufacturing adversaries.
clips.source_hint: /g/ thread on X Corp lawsuits against Nitter and forks popping up anyway

clips.text_zh: 歐美將啲工廠晒搬晒去晒中國，搞到自己連稀土都攞唔到。打仗都冇子彈出🇺🇸 真係識條鐵⋯⋯HK地產佬都係靠大陸貨。
clips.text_en_b1: Deindustrialization in Western countries has ruined their future. If you want to wage war, you need factories running. They outsourced everything from clothes to missiles and now only have worthless pieces of paper. Europe attacked Russia and lost energy. The U.S. attacked China and can't get rare earths.
clips.text_en_b2: Deindustrialization has effectively gutted the West's strategic capacity. If you want to wage a serious war, you need factories humming around the clock, yet Europe and the US outsourced everything from clothing to missile components. Now they're left holding worthless pieces of paper instead of supply chains. Europe picked a fight with Russia and lost access to energy, while the US picked a fight with China and can't secure rare earths.
clips.text_en_c1: The systematic deindustrialisation of the Western economies has, by virtually any historical reckoning, mortgaged their long-term strategic position. Decades of outsourcing, ranging from textiles to advanced munitions, have left America and Europe perilously dependent on adversarial supply chains. The Europeans, having provoked Russia, consequently endured an energy catastrophe; the Americans, having provoked China, now find themselves unable to procure the rare earths that modern warfare demands. The factory floors have been hollowed out, leaving nothing but depreciating paper currency in their stead. Even Hong Kong's property magnates, for their part, remain tethered to mainland manufacturing output.
clips.text_en_c2: The systematic deindustrialization pursued by Western economies over successive decades may well prove to have bequeathed them a strategically untenable inheritance. Manufacturing capacity—from apparel to advanced munitions—was ceded, almost as a matter of ideological consensus, to jurisdictions whose geopolitical alignment has since deteriorated. The ramifications are now manifesting with uncomfortable clarity: a Europe that sanctioned Russia discovered itself bereft of affordable energy, while a United States that antagonized China discovered, rather abruptly, that its rare earth supply chains had atrophied into near-irrelevance. What remains, in essence, is a portfolio of paper assets whose utility in sustaining industrial output is approximately nil. Hong Kong's property magnates, meanwhile, depend on precisely the mainland supply networks now weaponized.
clips.source_hint: /pol/ thread blaming Western deindustrialization for loss of war-making capacity

Anime aficionados, it must be said, approach such discussions with a taxonomical zeal that Western gaming discourse rarely matches. clips.text_zh: 又話深蹲係meme lift。古希臘人根本唔做squat，佢哋跑同揹重嘢。我同肥仔信都係leg day靠carries lol，問我點解無 thigh growth 🧐
clips.text_en_b1: Squats are a meme lift prioritized way too much in modern lifting. The ancient Greeks didn't do squats. They ran for legs and lifted heavy things for upper body. They carried heavy things for legs but never squatted. Bench, OHP, deadlift, running, and carries cover everything.
clips.text_en_b2: Squats are massively overrated in modern lifting culture, and calling them a meme lift isn't entirely unfair. The ancient Greeks, who built impressive physiques without gym machines, never actually squatted with a barbell. They relied on running to develop their legs and on heavy carries for full-body strength, alongside overhead pressing and deadlifting for the upper body. Honestly, bench, OHP, deadlifts, running, and loaded carries cover just about everything.
clips.text_en_c1: The veneration of squats within contemporary lifting culture is, I would argue, considerably overblown. The ancient Greeks, whose physiques remain the object of widespread admiration, eschewed barbell squats entirely. Their lower-body conditioning derived from sustained running and loaded carries, while upper-body strength was cultivated through heavy stone and sandbag work. They transported substantial loads on foot yet never descended into a parallel squat, a fact that should give pause to those who treat the movement as sacrosanct. Bench, overhead press, deadlifts, running, and farmer's carries collectively furnish a far more comprehensive template.
clips.text_en_c2: The veneration of squats within contemporary strength training culture warrants considerably more scrutiny than it typically receives, since the movement occupies a disproportionate share of programming templates whose efficacy remains, at best, contested. The ancient Greeks, whose physical exemplars we nevertheless claim to emulate, apparently eschewed the exercise altogether; their lower body development derived from extended locomotion and weighted ambulation, while their upper bodies were forged through loaded carries and pressing movements of various descriptions. Bench press, overhead press, deadlift, distance running, and farmer's carries, properly programmed, arguably furnish a more comprehensive stimulus than the barbell back squat's devotees typically acknowledge. The leg day protocol need not, in other words, revolve around a single pattern.
clips.source_hint: /fit/ contrarian thread arguing carries and running beat squats for leg development

clips.topic_en: Why Buy BTC After The Pump
clips.text_zh: 成日都係咁。睇住 BTC 喺度 sideways 兩三個禮拜，零興趣，然後佢一抽 15%，個個就衝入場。到底 why？每次都係咁，fomo 死晒 🙏 入都入遲，止蝕都唔知擺邊
clips.text_en_b1: You watch BTC do nothing for weeks and ignore it completely. Then it pumps 15% and suddenly everyone wants in. Why does everyone want to buy after the move already happened? The chart sits flat, nobody cares, one green candle and Twitter fills up with new buyers. FOMO in full force every single time.
clips.text_en_b2: Bitcoin sits sideways for a couple of weeks, and absolutely nobody gives a damn. The moment it suddenly pumps around 15%, though, everyone rushes in trying to chase the move. Why does this pattern keep repeating itself without fail? One green candle appears, and Twitter immediately fills up with fresh buyers piling in long after the breakout. Classic FOMO behaviour every single time, and by then the easy gains are already gone.
clips.text_en_c1: It happens with such monotonous regularity that one could almost set a calendar by it. Bitcoin sits in a prolonged sideways drift for two or three weeks, attracting virtually no interest whatsoever, and then a single 15% vertical move drags every sidelined retail participant back into the market in a frenzy. The irony, of course, is that by the point at which sentiment has shifted, the low has long since been left behind; what remains is the elevated entry, the late chase, and the inevitable question of where, if anywhere, one ought to place a stop. Classic FOMO in its purest form.
clips.text_en_c2: There exists a remarkably consistent pattern in retail crypto behaviour that borders on the pathological. Bitcoin drifts sideways for weeks on end, volume evaporates, and not a soul deigns to glance at the chart. Then a fifteen-percent wick materialises almost out of nowhere, and the very same individuals who previously yawned at consolidation come flooding back, licking their chops at what they imagine is a fresh opportunity. The irony is almost poetic: by the time price action has already delivered, positioning has become the worst it could possibly be, since the only people still buying are precisely those who should have been accumulating when nobody cared. Twitter fills with triumphant declarations, Telegram groups spawn anew, and somehow FOMO remains the most reliable contrarian indicator the market has ever produced.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ thread complaining about post-pump FOMO buying

clips.text_zh: 成日見到人話 '你試咗 paid model 未？你要試 ChatGPT Claude 先知幾恐怖'。點解從來冇人叫大家去用 Kimi、GLM、Qwen？cheap model 已經做到 90% 效果，得 10% 價錢喎。Ai 咁燒錢真係頂唔順
clips.text_en_b1: Anons keep saying 'you have not tried the paid model yet, try ChatGPT or Claude and you will see how scary they are.' But nobody ever tells people to spend less on cheaper models like Kimi, GLM or Qwen, which give about 90% of the performance for maybe 10% of the price. Has anyone else noticed this pattern?
clips.text_en_b2: Anons keep insisting that paid models like ChatGPT or Claude are on another level entirely, yet nobody bothers to recommend cheaper alternatives such as Kimi, GLM or Qwen. These budget options already deliver around 90% of the performance for roughly a tenth of the price, which makes the constant push toward expensive subscriptions feel somewhat suspicious. Has anyone else picked up on this pattern, or am I imagining things?
clips.text_en_c1: There is a curious pattern that anyone who spends time on these boards cannot have failed to notice: users perpetually insist that one must sample the premium tier, that ChatGPT or Claude will fundamentally recalibrate one's expectations of what an LLM can do. What nobody ever volunteers, however, is that models like Kimi, GLM and Qwen already deliver somewhere in the region of 90% of that performance for roughly a tenth of the subscription cost. Given how catastrophically capital-intensive inference has become, one might reasonably ask why this alternative is so rarely championed.
clips.text_en_c2: It is a curious phenomenon, one that recurs with almost mechanical regularity in certain online communities: whenever the subject of large language models arises, there is invariably some interlocutor eager to insist that one simply must experience the paid tier, that ChatGPT or Claude will reveal how terrifyingly capable these systems truly are. What is conspicuously absent from such evangelism, however, is any meaningful advocacy for the open-weights alternatives — Kimi, GLM, Qwen — models that, by most objective benchmarks, deliver somewhere in the region of ninety percent of frontier performance at perhaps a tenth of the monthly subscription cost. Whether this omission stems from genuine ignorance, reflexive brand-loyalty, or simply the algorithmic incentives that reward endorsing expensive incumbents is debatable, but the pattern itself is unmistakably consistent.

The downstream implications are rather staggering: one can reasonably anticipate Apple Coin, Google Coin, Microsoft Coin, and presumably an X Coin flooding the marketplace, fragmenting what was once a comparatively unified dollar ecosystem into a constellation of branded digital cash. Bitcoin languishes in a protracted period of consolidation for weeks on end, drawing virtually no interest from retail participants whatsoever. Then the moment price appreciates by a mere fifteen percent, the same crowd that dismissed it moments earlier scrambles to establish positions. If the move has already occurred, what exactly is the rationale for entry at that juncture? It essentially means those who end up underwater are invariably the ones who arrive at the party considerably after the host has left. The asymmetry is almost mathematical in its cruelty.
clips.text_en_c2: Why does Bitcoin suddenly become irresistible only after it has already risen? One watches it stagnate for several weeks, apparently devoid of momentum, while scarcely anyone pays attention; then, almost overnight, the price inflates by fifteen per cent and the previously indifferent rush to buy in. This recurrent inversion—during which BTC is treated as though it were dead before its advance, then embraced with the ardour of a new convert once the move has occurred—is precisely what turns ordinary holders into involuntary passengers on a sinking ship. clips.text_en_b1: Redpill me on buying Cybercabs and putting them to work on the Tesla Robotaxi network for passive income. How much does each unit cost, what's the realistic payback period, and does the math actually work after insurance and maintenance?
clips.text_en_b2: I'm trying to get a realistic picture of the Cybercab opportunity before I throw any capital at it. Putting one of these units on the Tesla Robotaxi network for passive income sounds appealing on paper, but I want to know the real numbers: how much does each vehicle actually cost, what is a sensible timeframe for breaking even, and after you factor in insurance premiums, charging costs, and ongoing maintenance, does the business case genuinely hold up?
clips.text_en_c1: The proposition of purchasing a Cybercab, deploying it onto Tesla's forthcoming Robotaxi network, and thereby generating a steady stream of residual income admittedly sounds rather appealing on paper. Before anyone commits capital, however, several variables warrant rigorous scrutiny: the per-unit acquisition cost, the projected amortisation timeline, and crucially whether the underlying unit economics remain viable once insurance premiums, routine maintenance, depreciation, and platform fees have been factored into the equation. Strip away the marketing veneer, run the numbers in good faith, and only then determine whether the thesis genuinely holds water.
clips.text_en_c2: The proposition is beguiling in its simplicity: acquire a Cybercab, enrol it in Tesla's nascent Robotaxi network, and thereafter collect what purports to be fully passive income while the vehicle earns its keep around the clock. Yet the arithmetic underpinning such fantasies tends to be conspicuously absent from the marketing materials. What, precisely, does a single unit cost at retail, and over what plausible horizon does the cumulative revenue exceed that outlay? Once insurance premiums, depreciation, software subscriptions, and routine maintenance are folded into the spreadsheet, the proposition frequently inverts from income stream to liability. The Tesla faithful are nevertheless eager to be redpilled — though one suspects the red pill, in this instance, dissolves on the tongue rather than illuminating anything. A sober unit-economics breakdown would be vastly more welcome than another glossy reveal.

It is now 10 years later and there are more radiologists now, in higher demand and earning much higher salaries than in 2016. Next up to embarrass himself on the world stage is probably Elon Musk.
clips.text_en_b2: Back in 2016, Geoffrey Hinton confidently predicted that AI would render radiologists obsolete within a five-to-ten-year window. Roughly a decade has now passed, and the specialty has not collapsed; in fact, demand has actually grown, with higher salaries and more positions filled than ever. Watching his interview back is genuinely cringeworthy, since he is now widely regarded as just another overhyped prophet. My money is on Elon Musk being the next figure to embarrass himself publicly in a similar fashion.
clips.text_en_c1: Back in 2016, Geoffrey Hinton, a figure widely regarded as one of the principal architects of modern deep learning, asserted with considerable authority that artificial intelligence would displace radiologists within a window of five to ten years. A full decade has since elapsed, and the actual outcome has proved rather different from what was forecast: demand for radiologists has in fact risen, salaries have appreciated substantially, and the discipline continues to expand. Such prognostications are best treated with measured scepticism. Should the next public embarrassment arise, my money would be on Elon Musk overpromising once again.
clips.text_en_c2: A decade ago, Geoffrey Hinton — a man routinely described, without irony, as the godfather of modern deep learning — took to a prominent stage and confidently prophesied that radiologists would be rendered obsolete within five to ten years, displaced by convolutional networks capable of inferring malignancy from pixels with superhuman fidelity. Ten years on, the specialty has not merely persisted but expanded: demand for qualified radiologists has surged, compensation has climbed appreciably, and the ranks of residency programmes have swollen rather than thinned. Watching Hinton revisit those remarks on camera is to witness a masterclass in dignified revisionism, delivered with the aplomb of a man accustomed to audiences suspending disbelief. The next luminary slated for comparable public discomfiture is, in all likelihood, Elon Musk, whose own predictions have aged with comparable grace.

The implicit thesis, that credentialed expertise insulates practitioners from algorithmic substitution more effectively than raw technical fluency, carries a certain grim resonance, and respondents express, with varying degrees of equanimity, their resignation to a labour market wherein competence alone no longer confers competitive moats.

The familiar taxonomy presents itself, endomorphs and skinny-fat ectomorphs alike, united in their gradual accommodation to fluorescent lighting and vending-machine cuisine. The poster himself, paradoxically, continues to attend the gym with sufficient diligence that even the uncharitable eye of the trainer has remarked upon his leanness, a development he greets with bemused disbelief. The thread lands hardest, naturally, on those grinding through licensure exams by candlelight.
clips.source_hint: /fit/ OP fears losing his physique after switching from college to office life.

clips.text_zh: 轉生、cheat、慢生活、惡役，書局同streaming全部係呢啲。Toyokeizai話係外國人帶嚟，我信一半lol。🧐
clips.text_en_b1: Anime is no longer made for Japanese audiences. Bookstores and streaming services are flooded with isekai reincarnation works. New releases keep using words like reincarnation, cheat, exile, villainess, and slow life. The Toyokeizai piece blames foreign demand for the plague.
clips.text_en_b2: It increasingly feels like anime is no longer being produced primarily for domestic Japanese audiences, because bookstores and streaming platforms alike are absolutely drowning in isekai reincarnation titles, with virtually every new release leaning on buzzwords like reincarnation, cheat, exile, villainess, and slow life. The Toyokeizai piece pins most of the blame on foreign demand, and although I am only half-convinced, the saturation is genuinely difficult to ignore.
clips.text_en_c1: A recent Toyokeizai piece has catalysed debate across /a/ regarding the creeping homogeneity of contemporary anime, which increasingly appears engineered for export markets rather than domestic audiences. Bookstore shelves and streaming catalogues alike are saturated with isekai reincarnation narratives, peppered with the now-familiar vocabulary of cheat abilities, political exile, villainess arcs, and the slow-life subgenre. The article attributes the glut principally to foreign demand, a thesis I find myself half-inclined to accept, given that domestic publishers have evidently decided that these formulae constitute the safest possible commercial bet.
clips.text_en_c2: The phenomenon catalogued across /a/ and substantiated, however tendentiously, by a Toyokeizai feature, has by now acquired the character of an industry in remission from any original impulse. The taxonomy of contemporary isekai proliferation has become almost self-parodic in its comprehensiveness: reincarnation, cheat abilities, exile narratives, villainess reversals, and the pastoral idylls of slow-life variants crowd both physical bookstore shelves and the algorithmic feeds of every major streaming platform. The Toyokeizai analysis apportions blame to foreign consumption patterns, a thesis that half-exculpates the domestic production apparatus even as it implicitly indicts an industry for abandoning its erstwhile audience. Whether the foreign-demand diagnosis survives scrutiny, or merely serves as a convenient alibi for creative exhaustion at home, is a question the thread entertains with appropriate scepticism.
clips.source_hint: /a/ thread discussing Toyokeizai article on isekai oversaturation and foreign demand.

clips.text_zh: 又係BTC，升完先嚟問點解唔早啲買。睇住佢橫行幾星期唔理，然後一抽15%個個衝入嚟，wtf。明明之前可以瞓住都唔睇，而家又FOMO。prop firm啲錢又燒緊，好煩。
clips.text_en_b1: Why do people buy BTC after the pump? You watch BTC do nothing for weeks and ignore it completely. Then it pumps 15% and suddenly everyone wants in. Why does everyone want to buy after the move already happened?
clips.text_en_b2: Honestly, this BTC behaviour drives me up the wall. For weeks it trades sideways and nobody gives a damn, then the moment it rips 15% out of nowhere, every Tom, Dick and Harry scrambles to get in. The irony is brutal, since you could've been completely indifferent before the breakout. This classic FOMO cycle never fails to amaze me, and meanwhile prop firms keep bleeding capital. Infuriating, really.
clips.text_en_c1: The pattern never ceases to infuriate me. Bitcoin grinds sideways for weeks on end, conspicuously devoid of momentum, and the prevailing consensus is to ignore it entirely. Then, the moment it rallies fifteen percent in a sustained leg up, everyone suddenly develops an urgent conviction that they cannot afford to miss the move. This Pavlovian response to momentum is textbook FOMO; nobody wanted exposure at consolidation, yet every latecomer now demands a seat at the table. The irony is that the trade was available to anyone with the patience to simply do nothing.
clips.text_en_c2: It beggars belief that anyone still falls for the same self-defeating cycle. Bitcoin had meandered sideways for what felt like an eternity — candlesticks doing nothing more interesting than minor consolidation — and the prevailing mood was one of studied indifference. Then, as if on cue, price ripped fifteen percent in short order, and the very same chorus of voices who had been dismissing it as a dead cat weeks earlier suddenly pivoted into full-throated FOMO, scrambling to chase entries at the worst possible moment. Meanwhile, the prop firm capital I allocated continues to bleed out in a slow, steady hemorrhage, which compounds the irritation tenfold. The whole exercise is a textbook case of the familiar behavioural trap, yet the participants never seem to learn.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ anon complains about retail buying BTC after the move

Call it a pipedream, though, since the chances of it actually getting there are laughable. On top of that, my CFD positions are deep in the red, so averaging down is absolutely off the table. Patience is wearing thin, honestly.
clips.text_en_c1: I've been accumulating Dogecoin with what can only be described as delusional optimism, currently sitting on 9,150 coins with an admittedly ambitious target of 25,000, a threshold at which, should the price somehow reach one pound, I could theoretically purchase a Toyota AE86. The plan hinges entirely on an outcome that virtually no sober analysis would endorse. My CFD positions are meanwhile bleeding capital steadily, which raises the uncomfortable question of whether doubling down on an already precarious position constitutes conviction or sheer obstinacy. Still, the AE86 dream persists, even if the timeline remains frustratingly hypothetical.
clips.text_en_c2: At present I am sitting on 9,150 DOGE, accumulated over a stretch of what can only be described as serendipitous bottom-fishing, and the ostensible objective is to amass the full 25,000 coins before the dénouement arrives. The thesis, if one can grace it with that word, hinges on DOGE miraculously reattaining parity with sterling, at which juncture the intended spoils are earmarked for a meticulously specified Toyota AE86. The dream remains, regrettably, a purely aspirational one, given that the concurrent CFD positions are already deep in the red and further averaging down would be an exercise in financial self-harm rather than prudent accumulation.

clips.text_zh: Debian俾印度人接咗手，即刻vibecoding成個OS，omg到底係咩玩法。AI取代programmer嘅嘢遲早到我。仲有GPU/RAM點解仲有貨畀散戶買？個個政府同公司都要AI啦，唔應該一早斷貨？搞到我好焦慮，考牌都未完。
clips.text_en_b1: DEBIAN NOW INDIAN AI SLOP. An Indian takes over the Debian project. They immediately begin vibecoding the entire operating system. HAHAHAHAHAHAHAHA. So what's the stable distro of the future, Mageia or OpenMandriva? Or something else?
clips.text_en_b2: So apparently Debian has been taken over by some Indian team, and they're already vibecoding the entire operating system. What on earth is going on with this project? AI replacing programmers has been creeping closer for a while, and this feels like yet another nail in the coffin. Meanwhile, GPUs and RAM remain inexplicably available to retail buyers despite every government and corporation stockpiling them. Honestly, it's giving me serious anxiety on top of my licensing exams.
clips.text_en_c1: So the Debian project has apparently fallen into Indian hands, and the immediate response has been to begin what can only generously be described as vibecoding the entire operating system into existence. If this is the trajectory, one has to wonder what the stable distribution landscape will resemble in five years, Mageia, OpenMandriva, or something else entirely. Beyond the distro question, the broader anxiety remains: if AI is genuinely displacing programmers at this pace, what happens to those of us still grinding through certifications? The GPU and RAM supply situation is equally baffling, given that every government and corporation is hoarding compute. Stock should have run dry months ago.
clips.text_en_c2: The unfolding spectacle of Debian effectively falling into Indian hands, whereupon the entire operating system is being effectively vibecoded into oblivion, is enough to make one despair for the future of free software. The moment the reins were handed over, what had been a painstakingly curated distribution began its precipitous descent into AI-generated slop of the most undistinguished variety. Meanwhile, the broader question of why consumer-grade GPUs and RAM remain even marginally available to ordinary buyers defies comprehension, given that every government apparatus and corporate behemoth is presently hoovering up the entire supply chain for their own AI ambitions. The resultant anxiety is palpable, particularly when one still has a driving licence to acquire.
clips.source_hint: /g/ thread on Debian leadership change and AI policy

clips.text_zh: 馬斯克又嚟搞事，話低生育率係因為18歲呢個魔術數字。佢話adult應該puberty就default，唔好信政府個arbitrary age。香港同美國都一樣，我30歲仲單身，真係靠AI續命。ok呢啲嘢睇完就算，繼續返屋企睇書。
clips.text_en_b1: Elon Musk doesn't get it. Low TFR and birth rates are due to the 18 magical age theory and child labor laws. By default, one is considered an adult at puberty. Any animal with secondary sexual characteristics is a mature adult, Adam Smith noted the profitable employment of young people.
clips.text_en_b2: Elon Musk is at it again, claiming that collapsing birth rates stem from what he calls the 18 magical age threshold. He basically argues adulthood should kick in at puberty by default, dismissing government age limits as arbitrary nonsense. Whether you're in Hong Kong or the States, the picture looks identical. I'm thirty, still single, and frankly leaning on AI companions just to cope. Anyway, I've had enough of this rabbit hole, back to my books.
clips.text_en_c1: Elon Musk is opining on demographics again, this time attributing collapsing fertility rates to what he calls the eighteen magical age theory, the notion that arbitrarily designating eighteen as the threshold of adulthood has somehow distorted the natural order. He appears to genuinely believe that puberty should default to adult status, a position that conveniently disregards centuries of labour law and developmental psychology. Meanwhile, I remain single at thirty in Hong Kong, increasingly reliant on AI for whatever passes for companionship these days. The discourse is exhausting, so I shall return to my books and pretend the broader civilisational trajectory is someone else's problem to solve.
clips.text_en_c2: Musk, characteristically, has once again weighed in on demographic collapse with characteristic provocation, positing that the precipitous decline in total fertility rates can be attributed to what he terms the 18-year magical age threshold. His argument, stripped of its contrarian varnish, runs that biological adulthood ought to be defined by puberty rather than by arbitrary legal convention, and that any creature exhibiting secondary sexual characteristics is, in essence, a mature adult. He invokes Adam Smith's observations on the profitable employment of young people as historical corroboration, though one suspects the parallel is doing rather more work than it ought. The debate, while intellectually stimulating, is ultimately academic.
clips.source_hint: /pol/ thread raging about Musk and age-of-majority laws

clips.text_zh: GTA 6個Lucia真係woke到爆。5尺2寸女仔一拳打低6尺3寸男人，又識開槍又識揸車，仲要單手裝shotgun。lol到底邊個寫嘅劇本？我打LOL打到S15都仲未上鑽，今日又要肥仔信叫我去gym。
clips.text_en_b1: GTA 6 is fine but Lucia is immersion breaking. She is 5 foot 2 and can knock out a 6 foot 3 man with one punch. She can shoot and drive at superhuman levels and even reloads shotguns with one hand. No one can realistically do these things, this is bullshit.
clips.text_en_b2: GTA 6 itself is solid, but Lucia honestly shatters any sense of immersion. The woman is 5'2" yet floors a 6'3" bloke with a single punch, handles firearms like a Navy SEAL, drives like a seasoned getaway driver, and somehow reloads a shotgun one-handed. Whoever greenlit this script clearly prioritised aesthetics over plausibility. Meanwhile, I've been grinding League of Legends stuck in Silver, and my mate keeps pestering me about hitting the gym.
clips.text_en_c1: GTA 6 is otherwise a competent title, but Lucia's characterisation has proven genuinely immersion-breaking for anyone with a rudimentary grasp of physical plausibility. She stands approximately five foot two, yet routinely incapacitates men exceeding six foot three with single punches, handles firearms with implausible proficiency, executes high-speed driving sequences that would challenge professional rally drivers, and, most egregiously, reloads a shotgun one-handed. Whoever drafted this script appears to have confused wish fulfilment with credible character writing. Separately, I have been grinding League of Legends through Season 15 without reaching Diamond, and today my friend insisted I start going to the gym, advice I will almost certainly ignore.
clips.text_en_c2: GTA 6, taken on its own merits, is a competent enough title; the grievance lies specifically with Lucia, whose portrayal is so egregiously calibrated to contemporary ideological sensibilities that immersion fractures almost immediately upon her introduction. The conceit that a woman standing five foot two can deck a man of six foot three with a single, unassisted punch strains credulity beyond any reasonable threshold, and her purported superhuman proficiency with firearms, motor vehicles, and the one-handed racking of a shotgun beggars belief entirely. One can only surmise that the writing staff prioritised a particular thematic agenda over the most rudimentary principles of internal consistency. The cumulative effect is one of being lectured at, rather than entertained, which is rarely the desired register.
clips.source_hint: /v/ thread complaining about GTA 6 protagonist Lucia

clips.text_zh: 3個月瘦45磅，但肌肉同力量都走晒。gym真係打到條命，唔夠氣又唔夠蛋白質。要forcefeed自己，whole meal都食唔晒。咁我點樣仲有錢join MMA？考牌進度零，prop firm又燒緊錢，thx真係廢柴。
clips.text_en_b1: How the FUCK are you able to lift heavy and get enough protein on this shit? I lost 45 pounds in 3 months but I definitely lost muscle and strength. Being at the gym kills me. I get fatigued as fuck. My heart gets raped by squats, I feel like I am going to die.
clips.text_en_b2: How on earth are people supposed to lift heavy and hit their protein macros while cutting this aggressively? I've shed 45 pounds in three months, but muscle and strength have absolutely evaporated along the way. Every gym session feels like a death sentence, I'm constantly gassed, and squats have my heart pounding out of my chest. Eating feels like forced labour since I can barely finish whole meals. Between MMA fees and prop firm burn, I'm cooked.
clips.text_en_c1: I dropped forty-five pounds over three months, which sounds commendable until you factor in the rather significant caveat that I have simultaneously sacrificed a substantial proportion of my muscle mass and baseline strength in the process. Training sessions have become genuinely punishing; the deficit leaves me chronically fatigued, my cardiovascular system protests every set of squats with what feels like mortal conviction, and I am perpetually forcing down meals I cannot reasonably finish in pursuit of adequate protein. The economics compound the misery: MMA memberships cost money I no longer have, licensing progress stands at precisely zero, and prop firm capital continues evaporating. Functional adult, evidently not.
clips.text_en_c2: The arithmetic of aggressive caloric deficit is, as ever, brutally straightforward but punishing in its execution. Over the course of three months I have shed forty-five pounds, a figure which on paper reads as unequivocal progress yet conceals a far more equivocal reality: lean mass has evaporated, maximal strength has cratered, and the residual fatigue is so pervasive that each successive gym session assumes the character of an existential ordeal. The cardiovascular strain imposed by even moderate squat work leaves one genuinely uncertain whether the next rep will be the last, whilst the perpetual necessity of force-feeding oneself sufficient protein to merely tread water becomes its own Sisyphean torment.
clips.source_hint: /fit/ anon struggling to lift heavy while cutting calories

clips.text_zh: 原版Mobile Suit Gundam真係被underrated，而家啲人一講就Zeta、ZZ、CCA嗰啲膠嘢。嗰啲唔同人做應該non-canon。我就鍾意00，認真睇完覺得係神作。返到HK之後都係得返睇anime打發時間，30歲仲單身，靠AI續命lol。
clips.text_en_b1: Is Mobile Suit Gundam underrated? Nowadays, most people can't discuss it without mentioning the dogshit sequels Zeta, ZZ, and CCA, which were made by completely different people and should be considered non-canon. It really devalues the original masterpiece.
clips.text_en_b2: Original Mobile Suit Gundam is genuinely underrated, since modern discourse inevitably derails into wanking over Zeta, ZZ, and CCA, which were essentially produced by entirely different teams and should arguably be treated as non-canon. Personally, I think Gundam 00 is the real masterpiece once you actually sit down with it. Back in Hong Kong, anime is basically my only pastime now that I'm thirty, single, and relying on AI to keep myself sane. Pathetic, I know.
clips.text_en_c1: The original Mobile Suit Gundam remains, in my estimation, a criminally undervalued work, one whose reputation has been quietly eroded by its own increasingly mediocre sequels. Any serious discussion today inevitably devolves into references to Zeta, ZZ, and Char's Counterattack, entries produced by largely different creative teams and, frankly, deserving of non-canonical status given their narrative inconsistencies. Personally, I find Gundam 00 to be the genuinely underappreciated masterpiece of the franchise, a position I will defend against any challenger. Back in Hong Kong, single at thirty, my leisure activities have narrowed to anime and AI companionship, a combination that sounds bleak but somehow suffices.
clips.text_en_c2: The original Mobile Suit Gundam, that urtext of the mecha genre, remains chronically and unjustly undervalued in contemporary discourse, eclipsed as it is by its purportedly superior successors. The prevailing critical consensus now treats Zeta, ZZ, and Char's Counterattack as essential continuations of the mythology, notwithstanding that they were helmed by entirely different creative personnel and consequently should be regarded, at best, as non-canonical apocrypha rather than legitimate scripture. This persistent conflation inevitably dilutes the stature of Tomino's original masterwork. Personally, I find myself gravitating towards Gundam 00, which upon a serious reappraisal reveals itself to be nothing short of a transcendent achievement in the genre, though I suspect such a heretical preference invites considerable opprobrium from the orthodox.
clips.source_hint: /a/ thread defending the original 1979 Gundam over its sequels

According to the OP, the price essentially flatlines for weeks and nobody bats an eyelid, yet once it pumps around 15% out of nowhere, FOMO kicks in and everyone rushes the exit door. clips.text_en_c1: An anon on /biz/ poses what is by now a rhetorical question: why does retail invariably chase Bitcoin immediately after the move? For roughly a fortnight, price action was directionless, and sentiment was apathetic; the moment BTC surged some fifteen percent, however, the very same participants who dismissed it scrambled to enter positions. The post crystallises a behavioural pattern that traders themselves acknowledge yet never seem to internalise. Whether this constitutes FOMO in its purest form or simply crowd-induced capitulation is, evidently, beside the point.
clips.text_en_c2: A /biz/ anon, palpably weary of the cyclical theatrics, poses what is by now a rhetorical inquiry: why does the retail cohort invariably capitulate to FOMO the moment Bitcoin registers a discernible move? The price idles, listless and unremarkable, for a fortnight; not a soul blinks. Then, with the predictability of a Greek tragedy, BTC surges fifteen percent and the platforms buckle under the weight of late entrants scrambling aboard a vessel that has, by definition, already departed. The poster observes, with no small measure of exasperation, that human nature — at least within this particular subreddit — appears constitutionally incapable of buying the rumour rather than the fact, of accumulating before the breakout rather than afterwards.

clips.text_en_c2: Two axioms that the crypto faithful have long treated as gospel appear, on current evidence, to be on a collision course. The first dictates that a decisive break above the daily 200-day simple moving average, following a prolonged downturn, inaugurates the subsequent bull cycle. If, as the price action now suggests, the cyclical low was registered around the fifty-eight thousand dollar threshold a mere two months past, then the preceding bear regime would have lasted barely six months — a duration wholly at odds with the roughly twelve-month baseline the community has internalised. clips.text_en_c1: For those who harbour lingering curiosity regarding The Big O, the Sunrise mecha-noir series remains a surprisingly rewarding watch decades on. The premise essentially asks what Batman might have been had he been written as a compelling protagonist rather than a brooding cipher, and the answer proves far more stylish than one might anticipate. Across its twenty-six episodes, the programme fuses the dramatic weight of retro-futuristic giant-robot combat with the moody atmospherics of classic detective fiction, and the genres coexist in a manner that ought by rights to feel incongruous yet somehow does not. https://boards.4chan.org/a/thread/290215188
clips.text_en_c2: The Big O occupies a peculiar and rather hallowed position within the pantheon of mecha-noir hybrids, a genre so underpopulated that virtually any addition to its canon is cause for quiet celebration among devotees. The premise, reduced to its essentials, asks a deceptively simple counterfactual — what might Gotham have resembled had its masked protector been marginally less brooding and substantially more competent at the actual business of crime-fighting? — and proceeds to answer it over the course of twenty-six episodes whose interplay between noir-inflected detective storytelling and lumbering giant-robot theatrics remains, to this day, remarkably deft. For those who came of age marinating in Gundam 00 and its ilk, the series retains an enduring nostalgic pull, and even viewed with contemporary eyes it withstands scrutiny with admirable composure.
